quests.sentence: She can speak three languages.
quests.ruleExplanation: Can speak expresses ability, with the base verb speak following can directly, and three languages as the object.
quests.nativeTip: Can sits right after the subject, before the base verb, to express ability.

quests.sentence: They can solve this problem quickly.
quests.ruleExplanation: Can solve keeps solve in base form, with this problem as the object and quickly (manner) closing the sentence.
quests.nativeTip: The base verb never changes after can, and a manner adverb can still close the sentence.

quests.sentence: He can operate heavy machinery.
quests.ruleExplanation: Can operate keeps operate in base form after He, with heavy machinery as the object.
quests.nativeTip: Can still sits right after the subject, before the base verb.

quests.sentence: He could read by the age of four.
quests.ruleExplanation: Could read expresses a past ability, with by the age of four (a time expression) closing the sentence.
quests.nativeTip: Could expresses ability in the past — same position as can, right before the base verb.

quests.sentence: They could hear the music from outside.
quests.ruleExplanation: Could hear expresses a past ability to perceive something, with the music from outside completing the sentence.
quests.nativeTip: The same past-ability pattern holds, with the base verb and object following could.

quests.sentence: Could you pass the salt, please?
quests.ruleExplanation: Could inverts to the front to form a polite request, and please, set off by a comma, softens the request at the end.
quests.nativeTip: Could also makes a polite request when inverted to open a question, with please softening it further.

quests.sentence: It may rain this afternoon.
quests.ruleExplanation: May rain expresses a possibility about the weather, with this afternoon (time) closing the sentence.
quests.nativeTip: May expresses possibility — it sits right after the subject, before the base verb.

quests.sentence: She might join us for dinner.
quests.ruleExplanation: Might join expresses a tentative possibility, with us for dinner completing the sentence.
quests.nativeTip: Might works like may, expressing a slightly less certain possibility, in the same position.

quests.sentence: They may need additional support.
quests.ruleExplanation: May need expresses a possible future need, with additional support (including an adjective) as the object.
quests.nativeTip: May still expresses possibility here, with an adjective inside the object phrase.

quests.sentence: You must wear a helmet here.
quests.ruleExplanation: Must wear expresses a strong obligation or rule, with a helmet here completing the sentence.
quests.nativeTip: Must expresses strong obligation — it sits right after the subject, before the base verb.

quests.sentence: Employees must complete the safety training.
quests.ruleExplanation: Must complete expresses a required action for Employees, with the safety training (a compound noun) as the object.
quests.nativeTip: The same obligation pattern applies to a group subject, with a compound-noun object.

quests.sentence: Visitors must sign in at reception.
quests.ruleExplanation: Must sign in uses a phrasal verb after must, with at reception (place) closing the sentence.
quests.nativeTip: Must still expresses obligation, even with a phrasal verb and a place phrase.

quests.sentence: You mustn't enter this area.
quests.ruleExplanation: Mustn't enter means the action is forbidden, a stronger meaning than simply 'not required' — compare this to don't have to in the next two sentences.
quests.nativeTip: Mustn't expresses prohibition — something that is not allowed, not simply unnecessary.

quests.sentence: You don't have to attend the meeting.
quests.ruleExplanation: Don't have to attend means the meeting is optional, the opposite meaning of mustn't, which would mean it's forbidden.
quests.nativeTip: Don't have to means something is optional, not forbidden — a very different meaning from mustn't.

quests.sentence: Employees don't have to work weekends.
quests.ruleExplanation: Don't have to work confirms that weekend work is optional for Employees, reinforcing the contrast between prohibition (mustn't) and no necessity (don't have to).
quests.nativeTip: The same 'optional, not forbidden' meaning applies here, contrasting with mustn't from the first sentence.

quests.sentence: She has to renew her license.
quests.ruleExplanation: Has to renew expresses a required action for She, with her license as the object.
quests.nativeTip: Has to expresses necessity for a singular subject, sitting right before the base verb.

quests.sentence: We need to finish this by Friday.
quests.ruleExplanation: Need to finish expresses a required action for We, with by Friday (a deadline) closing the sentence.
quests.nativeTip: Need to expresses a similar necessity, with a time expression closing the sentence.

quests.sentence: They have to submit the paperwork today.
quests.ruleExplanation: Have to submit expresses a required action for They, with the paperwork as the object and today closing the sentence.
quests.nativeTip: Have to works the same way for a plural subject, with a time word at the end.

quests.sentence: You should see a doctor.
quests.ruleExplanation: Should see gives advice, with a doctor as the object, following the usual modal-plus-base-verb pattern.
quests.nativeTip: Should sits right after the subject, before the base verb, to give advice.

quests.sentence: I would recommend this restaurant.
quests.ruleExplanation: Would recommend expresses a polite opinion, with this restaurant as the object.
quests.nativeTip: Would sits in the same slot to express a polite opinion or suggestion.

quests.sentence: She would love to visit Japan.
quests.ruleExplanation: Would love to visit combines would with an infinitive verb pattern, expressing a wish, with Japan as the destination.
quests.nativeTip: Would plus an infinitive expresses a wish or desire, a slightly different job for would.

quests.sentence: He might not attend the ceremony.
quests.ruleExplanation: Might not attend keeps might and not as separate words, expressing an uncertain negative possibility, with the ceremony as the object.
quests.nativeTip: Might not stays as two separate words (unlike mightn't, which is rarely used), right before the base verb.

quests.sentence: I wouldn't recommend that approach.
quests.ruleExplanation: Wouldn't recommend fuses would and not into one word, expressing a negative opinion about that approach.
quests.nativeTip: Wouldn't fuses would and not, expressing a negative opinion or recommendation.

quests.sentence: You shouldn't ignore the symptoms.
quests.ruleExplanation: Shouldn't ignore fuses should and not, giving negative advice about the symptoms.
quests.nativeTip: Shouldn't works the same way, expressing negative advice right before the base verb.

quests.sentence: May I ask you a question?
quests.ruleExplanation: May moves ahead of I to politely ask for permission, with ask you a question following in its usual order.
quests.nativeTip: May inverts to the front to politely ask for permission, before the subject and base verb.

quests.sentence: Would you mind closing the window?
quests.ruleExplanation: Would leads the question before you, and mind closing the window follows as a very polite way to make a request.
quests.nativeTip: Would inverts the same way to make an extremely polite request.

quests.sentence: Must we finish this today?
quests.ruleExplanation: Must opens the question before we, asking whether finish this today is truly required.
quests.nativeTip: Must can also invert to ask whether something is truly necessary.

quests.sentence: New employees must complete orientation before they start working.
quests.ruleExplanation: Must complete expresses a required action, and before they start working names the later event this obligation must be finished ahead of.
quests.nativeTip: Combine must (obligation) with a before-clause naming what comes after it in the sequence.

quests.sentence: You don't have to submit the form until Friday.
quests.ruleExplanation: Don't have to submit shows the action is optional for now, with until Friday marking the point when it becomes due.
quests.nativeTip: Combine the negative no-necessity form with a time expression marking the deadline.

quests.sentence: She might need extra time to prepare her presentation.
quests.ruleExplanation: Might need expresses a possible requirement, and to prepare her presentation (an infinitive of purpose) explains why the extra time is needed.
quests.nativeTip: Combine might (possibility) with an infinitive phrase expressing purpose.
